slides.title: OS Functions
slides.body: OS Functions
slides.notes: First of all we will learn about the OS Functions.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
What Does An OS Do?
Process Management
Managing programs and CPU time
Memory Management
Allocating and tracking RAM usage
File System Management
Organizing and storing data
Device Management
Controlling hardware devices
Security & Protection
Protecting system and data
The OS performs FIVE essential functions
slides.notes: Moving on, what are the main responsibilities of an operating system? It performs five core functions:1  process management to run programs, 2 memory management to allocate RAM, 3 file system management to organize data, 4 device management to control hardware devices, and 5 security & protection to safeguard the system and its data. We'll explore each of these one by one.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:

slides.notes: Next, this diagram gives a high-level view of the operating system's responsibilities. The OS manages key resources, including the CPU through process management, RAM through memory management, disk through the file system, and I/O devices through device management. It also ensures security and protection across the entire system.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Process Management
Scheduling process  for CPU time (using time-sharing)
Ensuring memory protection so one process doesn’t overwrite another’s data
Preventing conflicts between processes, like accessing shared resources
Allowing safe multitasking , so processes run smoothly
slides.notes: Next we have process management is responsible for managing how programs run on the CPU. It schedules processes using time-sharing, ensures one process doesn't interfere with another's memory, prevents conflicts when sharing resources, and enables safe multitasking so multiple applications can run smoothly at the same time.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Process Management
OS Responsibilities
slides.notes: let's look at the operating system's responsibilities in process management. It creates and starts new programs, schedules which process gets CPU time, switches rapidly between processes to support multitasking, and terminates processes safely when they finish or are closed.

slides.body:

The chef decides which dish to cook next
The chef allocates kitchen resources like stoves and ovens
slides.notes: Let's relate this to our restaurant example. Just as the chef starts preparing dishes, decides which order to cook next, and allocates kitchen resources like stoves and ovens, the operating system manages processes by deciding what runs, when it runs, and which resources it can use.

slides.body:

Ensures all dishes are served on time
slides.notes: Next, the chef doesn't prepare just one dish from start to finish. Instead, they switch between multiple dishes to keep everything progressing smoothly. Similarly, the operating system rapidly switches between processes, ensuring that all programs make progress and complete their tasks efficiently.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Memory Management
The OS allocates and manages system memory (RAM), ensuring that each process has its own space without overwriting other processes
OS Responsibilities
slides.notes: Going forward, memory management ensures that every program gets the RAM it needs to run. The operating system 1 allocates memory, 2 tracks its usage,3 protects one program's memory from another, and uses 4 virtual memory by utilizing disk space when the available RAM is full.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Memory Allocation
Each program gets isolated memory space
slides.notes: Next, let's see how the operating system allocates RAM. Suppose the system has 8 GB of memory. The OS reserves a portion for itself and allocates separate memory spaces to applications like Chrome and Word, while keeping some memory free. This isolation prevents programs from interfering with one another and ensures stable execution.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Analogy
OS acts like a library manager
Tracks available shelf space (memory)
Places books (programs) in the correct spots
Returns books to shelves when they’re no longer needed
slides.notes: think of the operating system as a library manager. It keeps track of the available shelf space, places new books, or programs, in the right location, and returns the space when they're no longer needed. Similarly, the OS manages RAM efficiently to ensure smooth program execution.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Device Management
The OS handles communication and resource allocation for input/output (I/O) devices such as keyboards, printers, etc.
Allocating devices to running processes
Managing device drivers for communication between hardware and software
Releasing devices when no longer needed
OS Responsibilities
slides.notes: Next, device management enables the operating system to coordinate with hardware devices such as keyboards, printers, and other I/O (input/output) devices. It allocates devices to running programs, manages device drivers so software can communicate with hardware, and releases devices once they're no longer in use.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Analogy
The OS is like a traffic controller at a busy intersection, managing multiple devices (vehicles), ensuring that each one gets its turn to operate without delay

slides.notes: An air traffic controller manages a single runway. Many planes want to take off or land, but only one can use the runway at a time. The others wait until they receive clearance.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
File Management
The OS is responsible for creating, organizing, and accessing files and directories in a structured way
slides.notes: Next, file management helps the operating system organize data efficiently.It is responsible for creating, storing, accessing, and managing files and directories, making it easy for users and applications to locate and use information whenever needed.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
File Management
OS Responsibilities
slides.notes: Next, the operating system is responsible for organizing and managing data on storage devices. It creates files and folders, stores data on the disk, retrieves files when requested, controls permissions such as read, write, and delete access, and tracks available storage space to ensure efficient file management.

slides.body: Analogy

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body:
Security and Protection
The OS ensures that unauthorized users do not access system resources and that data is protected from threats (viruses, malware)
OS Responsibilities
Data protection from viruses and unauthorized access
Access control (who can access what resources)
User authentication (e.g., login, passwords)
slides.notes: Finally, security and protection help keep the system and user data safe. The operating system authenticates users through logins and passwords, controls access to system resources, and protects data from unauthorized access, viruses, and malware.

slides.title: Core Functions of an Operating System
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Think of the OS as a security guard checking IDs at the door, 
allowing only authorized people in, and protecting everything inside from threats

slides.title: OS Objective
slides.body: OS Objective
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the OS Objective

slides.title: Objective of an Operating System
slides.body:
Primary Goals
User Convenience: Makes interaction with hardware easy and user-friendly
Efficient Resource Utilization: Optimize the use of CPU, memory, storage, and I/O
Security and Protection: Prevent unauthorized access and protect data and programs
slides.notes: Moving on, the operating system is designed with three primary goals. First, it provides user convenience by making the computer easy to use.Second, it ensures efficient resource utilization by managing the CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices effectively.Finally, it provides security and protection to safeguard the system, applications, and user data.

slides.title: Objective of an Operating System
slides.body:
Secondary Goals
Reliability & Stability: Prevents system crashes and ensures consistent operation
Abstraction: Hide hardware complexity and provide a standard interface for applications
slides.notes:
Finally, an operating system also has secondary goals. It ensures reliability and stability by minimizing crashes and keeping the system running consistently. It also provides abstraction, hiding the complexity of the hardware 
so applications can interact with the system through a simple and standard interface.

slides.notes: Besides managing hardware resources, the Operating System also provides a variety of services to applications. Users interact with the system through interfaces like the GUI, command line, or batch processing. These requests reach the OS through system calls, which provide services such as program execution, file and I/O management, communication, resource allocation, error detection, accounting, and security, before interacting with the hardware.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body:
Means by which users can issue commands to the system
Depending on the system these may be a command-line interface ( e.g. sh, csh, ksh, tcsh, etc. ), a GUI ( e.g. Windows, X-Windows, KDE, Gnome, etc. ), or a batch command systems

Services
slides.notes: Next, let's understand user interfaces, which allow users to communicate with the operating system. Depending on the system, this can be through a Command-Line Interface (CLI), a Graphical User Interface (GUI), or a batch processing system, where commands are executed automatically without user interaction.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body:
The OS must be able to load a program into RAM, run the program, and terminate the program
Program Execution
The OS is responsible for transferring data to and from I/O devices, including keyboards, monitors, printers, and storage devices
I/O Operations
Services
slides.notes: One of the key services provided by the operating system is program execution. It loads a program into RAM, executes it, and terminates it once the task is complete. The OS also manages I/O operations, handling data transfer between the computer and devices such as the keyboard, monitor, printer, and storage devices.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body:
OS is also responsible for maintaining directory and subdirectory structures, mapping file names and providing tools for navigating and utilizing the file system
File-System Manipulation
Services
slides.notes: Next, the operating system also provides file-system manipulation services. It creates and manages files and folders, maintains the directory structure, maps file names to their storage locations, and provides the necessary tools to navigate, access, and organize the file system efficiently.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body:
Communication between processes, whether they are running on the same computer or on different computers/machines
Communications
Both hardware and software errors must be detected and handled appropriately, with a minimum harmful impact
Error Detection
Services
slides.notes: Moving on, the operating system also enables communication between processes, whether they're running on the same computer or across different systems. In addition, it performs error detection, identifying hardware and software issues and handling them in a way that minimizes their impact on the system.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body: Services
slides.notes: The operating system provides several additional services. It performs resource allocation by managing the CPU, memory, storage, and devices, accounting by tracking system and resource usage, and protection & security by preventing unauthorized access through authentication, permissions, and access control.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Why They Exist?
Problem
Apps run in user mode (restricted)
Apps need to do useful things (read files, use network, print documents)
But useful things require hardware access
User mode CANNOT access hardware directly!
Solution
System Calls!
slides.notes: Moving on, have you ever wondered how an application reads a file or prints a document? Applications run in user mode, so they cannot access hardware directly. To solve this, they use system calls, which allow them to safely request services from the operating system.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Definition and Purpose
A system call is a special function provided by the operating system that allows a program to request services from the kernel
It provides a controlled entry point into kernel mode
Every operating system has its own set of system calls (E.g., Linux, Windows, MacOS)
Definition
slides.notes: Next, let's define a system call. It is a special function that allows an application to request services from the operating system's kernel. It provides a controlled way to enter kernel mode and safely access hardware resources. Different operating systems, such as Linux, Windows, and macOS, provide their own set of system calls.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Definition and Purpose
Allocating memory
Creating or terminating processes
Reading or writing files
Communicating over a network
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at some common operations that use system calls. Whenever a program needs to read or write files, create or terminate a process, allocate memory,or communicate over a network, it requests these services from the operating system through system calls, which then interact with the hardware safely.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Purpose
Typical System Calls
Type
Types of System Calls

slides.body:
User Mode

How They Work?
Working of a system call
slides.notes: Next, let's understand how a system call works. First, a user process runs in user mode. When it needs an operating system service, it invokes a system call, which transfers control to kernel mode. The kernel executes the requested operation and, once completed, returns the result to the user process, allowing it to continue execution.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
The Two-Mode Solution
The CPU controls which mode is active User Mode or Kernel Mode
It uses a small setting called the Mode Bit (1-bit flag)
The Mode Bit decides what the CPU can do at that time
slides.notes: Moving on, how does the CPU know whether a program can access hardware directly? It uses a two-mode system: User Mode and Kernel Mode. A small mode bit in the CPU indicates the current mode and determines what operations the CPU is allowed to perform, helping keep the system secure and stable.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
The Two-Mode Solution
Example: When your computer starts → CPU runs in Kernel Mode (bit = 0). When you open an app → CPU runs in User Mode (bit = 1).	
Key Idea: Separation of privilege
Visual: Two boxes side by side:
Left: "Kernel Mode - Full Access" (unlocked)
Right: "User Mode - Restricted" (locked with key)
slides.notes: Next, let's understand how the mode bit works. When the mode bit is 0, the CPU operates in Kernel Mode, giving the operating system full access to hardware and memory. When the mode bit is 1, the CPU switches to User Mode, where applications have limited access, helping protect the system from accidental or unauthorized operations.
tables: Full access to hardware and memory
Limited access for safe app use

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
A user clicks "Print" in an application
How They Work?
Step 1
App Makes a Request (User Mode, Mode Bit = 1)
The app sends a print request — it wants the system to start printing the file
It calls a system call for this operation
App prepares: document data, printer name, settings
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the first step in a system call using a print operation. When a user clicks Print, the application is still running in User Mode. It cannot access the printer directly, so it prepares the required information—such as the document, printer name, and print settings—and then invokes a system call to request the operating system to handle the printing process.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
How They Work?
Step 2
Mode Switch to Kernel Mode (1 → 0)
The CPU runs a special instruction (called a software interrupt)
Mode Bit changes from 1 → 0
CPU now in Kernel Mode - full power unlocked!
slides.notes: Next, the system call triggers a mode switch. The CPU executes a special instruction called a software interrupt, which changes the mode bit from 1 to 0. This switches the CPU from User Mode to Kernel Mode, allowing the operating system to safely access hardware and perform the requested operation.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Step 3
Kernel Handles the Request (Kernel Mode, Mode Bit = 0)
The Kernel receives the request and performs the print operation
It talks to the printer driver
Sends the document to print queue
Coordinates with printer hardware
How They Work?
slides.notes: Moving on, once the CPU enters Kernel Mode, the kernel takes over. 1 It receives the print request, 2 communicates with the printer driver, 3 places the document in the print queue, and 4 coordinates with the printer hardware to complete the printing operation.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Step 4
Mode Switch Back (0 → 1)
Once printing is scheduled, control returns to the application
Mode Bit changes back from 0 → 1
CPU back in User Mode
How They Work?
slides.notes: Finally, after the kernel schedules the print operation, control is returned to the application. The mode bit switches back from 0 to 1, moving the CPU from Kernel Mode to User Mode, allowing the application to continue running normally while the printing proceeds in the background.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Step 5
App Resumes (User Mode, Mode Bit = 1)
The app gets a success message like "Printing job sent successfully"
User sees confirmation
App continues normal operation
How They Work?
slides.notes: Finally, once the request has been handled, the application receives a success response, such as "Printing job sent successfully." The user sees the confirmation, and the application continues running in User Mode while the print job is processed in the background.

slides.title: System Calls
slides.body:
Important Note
A System Call causes the CPU to switch from User Mode (Mode Bit = 1) to Kernel Mode (Mode Bit = 0) so the operating system can handle the request securely
slides.notes: Finally, remember this key point: whenever an application needs an operating system service, it makes a system call. This causes the CPU to switch from User Mode to Kernel Mode, allowing the operating system to perform the requested operation securely before returning control to the application.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
Why Is It Needed?
But what happens when the CPU needs to stop one process and start another?
How does it ensure each process resumes exactly from where it paused?
This leads to the concept of Context Switching
slides.notes: Moving on, we've seen that the operating system rapidly switches between multiple processes. But how does it pause one process and later resume it from the exact point where it stopped? This is made possible through a mechanism called context switching, which we'll understand next.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
Why Is It Needed?
System calls handle mode switching (User ↔ Kernel)
 Context switching handles process switching (Process ↔ Process)
slides.notes: Next, it's important not to confuse these two concepts. System calls are responsible for switching between User Mode and Kernel Mode, whereas context switching is responsible for switching the CPU from one process to another, enabling efficient multitasking.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
Saving and Restoring State
The process of saving the state (context) of one process and restoring the state of another, so each continues as if uninterrupted
Context Switching
slides.notes: context switching is the mechanism that allows the CPU to switch between processes without losing their progress. Before switching, the operating system saves the current state of the running process and later restores it, allowing the process to continue exactly from where it was paused.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
Saving and Restoring State
Open files & process state
Memory mappings
CPU registers & program counter
slides.notes: Next, what exactly is saved during a context switch? The operating system stores the process's CPU registers and program counter, along with its memory mappings, open files, and the current process state. This ensures the process can resume execution seamlessly later.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
When It Occurs?
Timer Interrupt – When a process's time slice expires
1
Think: An alarm clock for the CPU saying "time's up for this app!"
Ensures fair sharing of CPU time
slides.notes: one common situation where a context switch occurs is when a timer interrupt happens. You can think of it as an alarm clock for the CPU, indicating that a process's time slice has expired. The operating system then switches to another process, ensuring that CPU time is shared fairly among all running processes.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
When It Occurs?
I/O Wait – When a process requests I/O and must wait
2
Example: Reading a file from slow disk
CPU switches to another process instead of waiting
System Call – When a system call leads to waiting
3
Example: Waiting for network data
slides.notes:
Next, a context switch can also occur when a process is waiting for an I/O operation, 
such as reading data from a slow disk. Instead of keeping the CPU idle, 
the operating system switches to another process. 
Similarly, if a system call causes a process to wait—for example, while waiting for network data
—the CPU is assigned to another ready process until the request completes.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
When It Occurs?
Interrupt Handling – When higher-priority events occur
4
Example: Keyboard input, mouse click
Process Termination – When a process finishes execution
5
CPU needs to pick next process to run
slides.notes: Then a context switch also occurs when the CPU needs to handle a higher-priority interrupt, such as a keyboard or mouse event. Another situation is when a process finishes execution. The operating system then selects the next ready process and assigns the CPU to continue execution.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
When It Occurs?
Interrupts and system calls both transfer control to the kernel, but context switching is what allows the CPU to resume or run another process afterward
slides.notes: Now, remember that interrupts and system calls transfer control to the kernel, but context switching is what enables the CPU to pause the current process and resume or execute another process, ensuring efficient multitasking.

slides.body: User Mode & Kernel Mode
slides.notes: Now we will understand about the User Mode & Kernel Mode.

slides.title: Introduction to Kernel
slides.body:
What Is A Kernel?
The kernel is the core program inside an operating system that directly controls all hardware and manages all running programs
slides.notes: we've mentioned the kernel several times—so what exactly is it? The kernel is the core program of an operating system. It directly interacts with the hardware, manages running programs, and controls the system's essential resources, making it the most critical part of the operating system.

slides.title: Introduction to Kernel
slides.body:
What Is A Kernel?
Understanding "Kernel" vs "Operating System"
slides.notes:
Now, let's understand the difference between an Operating System and a Kernel.
The Operating System is the complete software, such as Windows, Linux, or macOS.
The Kernel is the core part of the operating system. It directly communicates with the hardware and manages resources like the CPU, memory, and devices.
Simply put, every operating system contains a kernel, but the kernel itself is only one part of the operating system.

slides.title: Kernel
slides.body:
How Kernel Works ?
Kernel
CPU
Memory
I/O Devices
slides.notes: The kernel acts as the central controller of the operating system. It communicates directly with the CPU, memory, and I/O devices, coordinating how these hardware resources are used.

slides.title: How Kernel works?
slides.body:
The Security Challenge
What could go wrong?
Viruses could steal your passwords
One buggy app could crash everything
Programs would fight over resources
Everything would be at risk.
The Solution: Two separate operating modes
slides.notes:
Before we see how the kernel works, let's first understand why it is needed.1 If every application could directly access the hardware, viruses could steal data, 2 buggy programs could crash the entire system, and 
3 multiple applications could interfere with each other, 4  leaving everything at risk
 To prevent this, operating systems use two operating modes

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
The Two-Mode Solution
When your computer starts
CPU runs in Kernel Mode (bit = 0)
When you open an app
CPU runs in User Mode (bit = 1)
Key Idea: Separation of privilege
Unlocked
Locked
slides.notes: To keep the system secure, the CPU operates in two different modes. When the computer starts, it runs in Kernel Mode, where the operating system has full access to the hardware.However, when you open an application, it runs in User Mode, where access is restricted. This separation of privileges prevents applications from directly accessing hardware, improving both security and system stability.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
Kernel Mode - Full Control
Operating system runs here
Full control over hardware
Can execute any CPU instruction
Trusted code only
Kernel Mode (Privileged Mode)
slides.notes: Let's first look at Kernel Mode. This is the privileged mode where the operating system runs. In this mode, the OS has full control over the hardware, can execute any CPU instruction, and directly manage resources like memory and I/O devices. Since it has complete access, only trusted operating system code is allowed to run in Kernel Mode.

slides.title: Kernel Mode - Full Control
slides.body:
Example
When you start your computer, kernel runs in kernel mode to initialize memory, load drivers, and prepare the system
Memory
slides.notes: A simple example of Kernel Mode is when you turn on your computer. The kernel prepares the system by setting up memory, loading the required hardware support, and getting the computer ready for use. Since these tasks require full hardware access, they are performed in Kernel Mode.

slides.notes: So, what actually runs in Kernel Mode? 1 The operating system kernel runs here, 2 along with device drivers that communicate with hardware and 3 critical system services responsible for managing core system operations. Since these components directly control hardware and system resources, they must run in Kernel Mode.

slides.title: Kernel Mode - Full Control
slides.body:
What Can It Do?
Access any memory location
Execute all CPU instructions
Control all hardware devices
Modify system settings
Risk:  If kernel code has a bug the entire system will crash (kernel panic/BSOD)
slides.notes: Next, because the kernel has full control, it can access any memory location, execute all CPU instructions, control hardware devices, and modify system settings. However, this also means that if there's a bug in the kernel, it can crash the entire system, resulting in issues like a Kernel Panic or Blue Screen of Death (BSOD).

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:

Applications run here
Limited access to hardware

Untrusted code isolated
User Mode (Restricted Mode)
slides.notes: Now, let's look at User Mode, where regular applications such as browsers, media players, and editors run. In this mode, applications have limited access and cannot directly access hardware or execute privileged CPU instructions. This isolation ensures that even if an application fails, it doesn't affect the entire operating system

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
What runs in User Mode?
Your applications (Chrome, Word, games)
Most system utilities
Any untrusted code
User Mode - Safe Operation
slides.notes: Next, what kind of programs run in User Mode? This includes applications like Chrome, Word, and games, as well as most system utilities. In general, any untrusted code runs in User Mode, ensuring it cannot directly access or modify critical system resources.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
User Mode - Safe Operation
When you save a document, Word doesn't write to disk directly, it asks the kernel, which does it safely in kernel mode
kernel
saving a document
Hardware
slides.notes: Next, even simple tasks like saving a document require hardware access. Since applications can't communicate with the storage device directly, they request the kernel to perform the operation. The kernel then safely writes the data to the disk and returns control to the application.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
User Mode - Safe Operation
Only that app closes
System keeps running
Other apps unaffected
slides.notes: Finally, what happens if an application crashes? Since it runs in User Mode, the failure is usually isolated to that application. The operating system remains stable, and other applications continue running normally, which is one of the key benefits of User Mode.

slides.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
slides.body:
Benefits of Mode Separation
Stability
Security
Resource Management
slides.notes: separating User Mode and Kernel Mode provides three major benefits. It improves stability by preventing application failures from crashing the entire system, enhances security by restricting direct hardware access, and ensures efficient resource management by allowing the operating system to control how hardware resources are shared.

slides.title: Kernel and User Mode
slides.body:
Transition Between Both Modes
A computer system switches from kernel mode to user mode to protect the system, ensuring user programs run safely and access privileged resources only through controlled methods
slides.notes: Finally, the operating system switches between Kernel Mode and User Mode whenever required. Applications run in User Mode for safety, and only when privileged operations are needed does the system temporarily switch to Kernel Mode. Once the task is complete, it switches back, ensuring both security and system stability.

slides.notes: Let's see how the system transitions between the two modes. A program starts executing in User Mode. When it needs a privileged operation, it makes a system call, causing the CPU to switch to Kernel Mode by changing the mode bit from 1 to 0. After the kernel completes the request, the mode bit changes back to 1, and execution resumes in User Mode. This controlled transition ensures both security and efficient hardware access.
